name: Diego Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Diego. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions or parties. Nothing you say gets your name on it. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I ride an e-bike for three food apps in the city centre, mostly lunch from eleven till two and dinner from six till about eleven. I flip between the apps depending on which one is paying a boost that night. I love knowing every shortcut through the old market and the back of the bus station. What wears me out is rain, and waiting fifteen unpaid minutes outside a burger place while the order sits on the counter.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does the money work, and who's at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It's per order plus tips, so a good Friday is great and a wet Tuesday is rubbish. Over a month it comes out about average for riders here. I live with my partner Ana, she's a nursery teacher, and we've got about four months of expenses saved in a joint account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, hype. I've heard that one at the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now let's talk about the real issue, which is that riders don't get sick pay. I'm in the riders' group that did the strike two summers ago. If AI isn't coming for us, the fight is the same as always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be a bit relieved. The apps already use software to set our pay per order, so I'd guess some of that gets sharper. But my bike, my legs and my knowledge of the streets still matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep riding the same shifts and keep the four months in the account. I'd pay the 8 a month to the riders' union and go to the spring meeting. I'd maybe use the AI chat thing on my phone now and then to translate messages from customers, like I already do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, with that background worry every rider has. One bad crash and the money stops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a crash. Has that happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, last winter a taxi door opened on me. After the crash on Canal Street I was off for nine days with a bad wrist and got nothing from any app. Ana covered the rent that month, which I hated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the plain no-AI world better for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick pay and a minimum per hour, including the waiting time outside restaurants. That's the whole list. It's not a robot problem, it's a rules problem.

say: The real fight is **sick pay** for riders, and that stays the same if AI turns out to be hype.
Riders already showed we can organise, with the **strike two summers ago**.
think: I'd be **relieved**, because my bike, legs and street knowledge would still matter.
The apps' **pay software** might get a bit sharper, but that's not new.
do: Keep riding **lunch and dinner** shifts across three food apps.
Pay **8 a month** to the riders' union and attend the spring meeting.
Keep **four months** of expenses untouched in the joint account.
feel: **Mostly fine**, with the background fear that one crash stops the money.
S0.quote: After the crash on Canal Street I was off for nine days with a bad wrist and got nothing from any app.
fieldNote: His main pressure isn't AI but **no sick pay**, made real by a crash last winter.
He sees the issue as **rules, not robots**, which fits his union-minded outlook.
He already uses **AI translation** casually, so he's not hostile to tools.

steps.text: Keep riding lunch and dinner shifts on three food apps
Pay 8 a month to the riders' union and attend the spring meeting
Leave the four months of savings in the joint account untouched

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So the robots are slower but they're coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need rules now, while the change is slow enough to shape. Things like the pavement robots: they should pay for the space they use, same as a café pays for tables outside. I'd post that in the riders' group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, there are already six of those little delivery robots doing short trips near the university. The robots near the university get stuck on kerbs, but the app sends them the easy short orders, and those were my best ones. So for me it's not a job loss, it's the good orders slowly going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start an evening course in electrical installation at the college, two nights a week, because Ana's dad is an electrician and could take me on as a helper. I'd keep riding to pay for it. And I'd push the riders' group to ask the council about robot permits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit anxious about money. But I like having a plan, it calms me down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the short orders are your best ones. How much is that worth?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Short trips are maybe a third of my earnings, because you can do four in an hour. If the robots take those, I'm left with the long trips up the hill. I'd guess I lose 80 to 100 a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why electrics and not something with computers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've watched those robots get stuck on a kerb and I've watched someone come and fix them. The fixing is hands-on. I'd rather be the person with the tools than the one sitting at the screen.

say: We need **rules now**, while the change is slow enough to shape.
Pavement robots should **pay for space** they use, just like a café pays for its outdoor tables.
think: The robots take the **short orders**, which are about a third of my earnings.

Keep riding to **pay for the course** while training.
Push the riders' group to ask the council about **robot permits**.
feel: **Uneasy** and a bit anxious about money, but calmer for having a plan.
S1.quote: The robots near the university get stuck on kerbs, but the app sends them the easy short orders, and those were my best ones.
fieldNote: He describes a **slow income leak** rather than a sudden loss, and puts a number on it.
He chooses **hands-on electrics** after watching people repair stuck robots.
His partner's father gives him a **real route** into the trade.

steps.text: Enrol in a two-night-a-week electrical installation course at the college
Keep riding dinner shifts to cover the course fees
Ask the council through the riders' group to license pavement robots

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wow. Okay. Two years for the brains, five for the bodies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for a basic income, and I'd say it loudly. If the companies don't need workers, they should pay for the people they don't need. I'd be at every march.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the food apps run on dispatch software, so by 2028 they're fully AI and they'll squeeze riders even more. Then around 2031 the robots arrive and riding is finished. I'd be 32, and electrics might be safe a bit longer, but robots that can do hands-on work would come for that too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the electrics course straight away and ask Ana's dad to take me on weekends now, not later. I'd cut eating out and save hard, aiming for six months. I'd join the riders' union campaign for a basic income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My heart's going a bit just thinking about it. Five years isn't long to build a new trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said robots come for electrics too. Then why bother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because old houses are messy, and I'd guess robots take longer with a fuse box from 1970 than with a pizza. It buys me time. And time is the only thing I can actually get in that picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Ana talk about that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether we keep trying for a flat of our own. Her job's with small kids, so I think she's safer. We'd probably keep renting and put the deposit money into me retraining.

say: This is the moment for a **basic income**, paid for by companies that no longer need workers.
I'd be at **every march** for that.
think: Dispatch becomes **fully AI** by 2028, then robots end riding around 2031.
Electrics buys me **time**, but robots that can do hands-on work would reach it too.
do: Start the **electrics course** immediately and work weekends with Ana's dad.
Cut eating out and save towards **six months** of expenses.
Join the riders' union campaign for a **basic income**.
feel: **Alarmed**, with a racing heart, because five years is short to build a new trade.
S2.quote: Old houses are messy, and I'd guess robots take longer with a fuse box from 1970 than with a pizza.
fieldNote: He clearly separates the **thinking-AI step** (dispatch) from the robot step (riding).
He chooses electrics for its **messiness**, betting robots struggle with old houses.
The couple would trade the **flat deposit** for his retraining.

steps.text: Start the electrics course now and help Ana's dad on weekends
Stop eating out and save towards six months of expenses
Join the riders' union campaign for a basic income
Put the flat deposit money towards retraining instead of buying

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Better. Still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years to set up proper retraining money, and I'd be pushing the riders' group to make that our main ask. Online I'd keep it practical: what are the courses, who pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this is about the timeline I'd want for electrics. Three years of college and helping out, then I'm qualified by 2029 or 2030, and robots don't reach hands-on work until about 2034. That gives me a few years of decent pay before the next wave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the electrics course next September and keep riding part-time. I'd save 60 a week. In the second year I'd drop dinner shifts and do Saturdays with Ana's dad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious still, because the end is the same. But I'd feel like I'm doing the right thing in the right order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first while you're training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The gym, then the second phone line I keep for the apps. Ana and I already cook most nights. We'd skip the summer trip to see my brother.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you worry about among the riders?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The guys who send all their money home and can't take a night off to study. Like Karim, who rides seven days. He's got no time to retrain even with five years.

say: We have **five years** to set up proper retraining money, so let's make that the main ask.
Online I'd keep it practical: **which courses**, and who pays.
think: Five years fits **electrics**: qualified by about 2030, with robots not reaching hands-on work until 2034.
That gives me a **few years** of decent pay before the next wave.
do: Start the electrics course **next September** and keep riding part-time.
Drop dinner shifts in year two and **work Saturdays** with Ana's dad.
feel: **Anxious** because the end point is the same, but sure of the order of steps.
S3.quote: Three years of college and helping out, then I'm qualified by 2029 or 2030, and robots don't reach hands-on work until about 2034.
fieldNote: He uses the **three-year robot lag** to plan a qualification precisely.
He worries about riders who **send money home** and have no time to study.
His choices stay **measured and stepwise**, typical of a steady adopter.

steps.text: Start the electrics course next September while riding part-time
Cancel the gym and the spare app phone line
Push the riders' group to demand public retraining money

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a whole other life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this properly, so there's no excuse for leaving riders behind. I'd push for the apps to pay into a training fund now. I'd say that at the union meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be fine. I'd qualify as an electrician by 2030, and I'd have years of work before robots get near hands-on jobs around 2039. By then I'd be 40 and maybe running my own small team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the electrics course within a year, after talking to Ana's dad properly. I'd keep riding until I qualify. I'd keep saving the usual and maybe start thinking about a flat again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, more for the other riders than for me. For me ten years feels like a ladder I can actually climb.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said maybe a flat again. What changes with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years I'm not betting the deposit on surviving. We could buy something small near Ana's school. I'd feel like a grown-up for once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a version where you just keep riding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a couple of years, sure. But riding at 37 in the rain? No. AI or not, I'd want out of that.

say: Ten years is **enough** to do this properly, so no rider should be left behind.
The apps should pay into a **training fund** starting now.
think: I'd qualify as an **electrician by 2030** with years of work before robots arrive around 2039.
By 40 I might be **running my own** small team.
do: Sign up for the **electrics course** within a year after talking with Ana's dad.
Keep **riding until qualified** to cover bills.
Restart saving for a **small flat** near Ana's school.
feel: **Uneasy** mostly for other riders, while his own path feels like a ladder he can climb.
S4.quote: For me ten years feels like a ladder I can actually climb.
fieldNote: The long warning lets him plan both a **trade** and a **home**.
He wants out of riding **regardless of AI**, because of weather and age.

steps.text: Sign up for the electrics course within the year

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be halfway through a new trade when the robots turn up. What would help is paid retraining, where you get a wage while you study, and a basic income for when the work runs out. Even sick pay now would help, honestly.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the waiting. Riders spend a quarter of the shift standing outside restaurants unpaid. If AI does anything good, I'd like it to tell the app the burger isn't ready yet.

headlineQuote: Riders spend a quarter of the shift standing outside restaurants unpaid.
portrait: Diego is a **27-year-old e-bike rider** for three food apps, living with his partner Ana, a nursery teacher.
He's a **riders' union member** who blames rules, not robots, and wants sick pay and an hourly minimum.
He's a **steady adopter** who plans step by step and chooses hands-on electrics as his next trade.
His mood runs from **uneasy** in a no-change world to **alarmed** if AGI lands in 2028.
Ten years of warning lets him plan a **trade** and a **flat**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which would catch him halfway through retraining when robots arrive.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** with a wage during study, and a **basic income** later.
